Welcome back, this week is a bit more Jam packed than usual, with 6 events. So today we'll hit the American events and come back tomorrow for the European events.

Another piece of tech that's become popular for Deadwalker Zombies is to give them the Never-dead buff. title: A Brush With Greatness - Finishing Kuri
content:
And so, here we are, after a long while, I am going to complete the write-up of Kuri (if you’ve been following me on other platforms, you’ll know that I actually finished Kuri a good while ago, but it turns out that to an avid pusher of the pigments, painting comes a little easier and quicker than writing; who would have thought? I’ve waffled on a good while in this column; future display painting projects will be quicker, I promise. All the same, let’s finish up the wonderful Kuri, shall we? 

The fur trim of the steppe hat, which I think is similar to a Deel Hat in the Mongolian tradition, was basecoated originally with Pro Acryl Caramel Brown. You might well accuse me of lacking imagination here, but next I built highlights on the top of each of the fur ridges using Caramel Brown mixed with Pro Acryl Ivory, at a ratio of about 3:1 (I eyeball all my paint mixes so I can’t give you a scientific recipe to follow; you’ll just have to trust me). It’s a simple way to highlight something, but it’s effective all the same. I went on with smaller and smaller highlight areas, with more and more Ivory in the mix, until eventually it was straightforwardly ivory on the highest parts. For the fleece cuff on the sleeve, I treated each “bobble” of wool like a separate spherical volume and highlighted them accordingly, with stippled lights on the top end of each. I used a few brown and yellow-brown speedpaints to glaze some slight filters to give the shadows a little more interest, before capping off the fur with some Pro Acryl Bright Ivory. 

Loading...

The yellow-gold details on the helmet were basecoated previously with Pro Acryl Dark Green Brown from the Flameon signature set; if you’re aware of Flameon then you’ll know that he’s an undisputed master of non-metallic metal painting, and his signature set contains just about everything you’ll need when it comes to painting very striking NMM golds. 

After the Dark Green Brown, I ascended to the next paint on the ladder, Pro Acryl Dark Orange Brown, covering all but the deepest shadows on the gold details. It’s important to leave some of the Dark Green Brown still showing to solidify and reinforce the greenish shadow golds get in natural light.

Loading...

I’m sure you’ll be absolutely blown away by the next paint on the docket; that’s right, it’s Fairy Pink- no, just kidding, it’s Pro Acryl Orange Brown, again applied over a smaller area than the last paint. It doesn’t look quite metallic yet, but as the contrast ramps up there’ll suddenly be enough that a switch will flip and your brain will think “bloody hell that does look like metal doesn’t it?”

I hop, skip, and jump over Caramel Brown and settle instead on Pro Acryl Bright Yellow Ochre and Pro Acryl Bright Pale Yellow, painting with fine lines all in the same direction, much as I did on the bust of Casca - the effect created resembles a metal surface that’s been polished. A final tiny highlight of pure Pro Acryl Bold Titanium White completes the metallic look.

Finishing touches are what really bring everything together. That’s probably the most obvious thing you’ve ever heard in your life, but even so, the tiny touches that make everything pop are the most important aspect of painting. The finishing touch for Kuri is definitely her bird, a fearsome hunting hawk looking exceptionally regal as it sits on her arm. The chest and belly I basecoated with Pro Acryl Dark Ivory, the beak with Vallejo Game Color Sun Yellow, and the back with Pro Acryl Dark Umber, applied through the airbrush. I highlighted the chest plumage in much the same way as the fur hat and fleece lining from previous steps, simply by adding progressively more Ivory to the Dark Ivory, before finishing off with Bright Ivory. I looked at some references and decided that it would be nice if the chest plumage had a bit of separation between the rows of feathers, so I used a bit of Caramel Brown to outline them a little, and then a little Army Painter Speedpaint Oak Brown to outline them even more.

Loading...
Eyes are one of my favourite things to paint, but they can no doubt be daunting. When it comes to birds’ eyes, treating the whole thing as one large iris is the way to go. I laid the foundation with some Pro Acryl Black Brown over the whole thing. Some Pro Acryl Coal Black in the centre forms the pupil. It’s really important to make sure that the light on the bird and the light on the girl are the same to avoid breaking the illusion, so with her as my guide, I painted increasingly small crescents of Orange Brown in the opposite corner, then Orange Brown mixed with some Pro Acryl Bright Yellow Ochre as a final bit of shine. To complete the illusion of the eye as being glassy and wet, I painted a large catchlight at the opposite corner using Pro Acryl Bold Titanium White. I shaded the majority of the beak using Army Painter Speedpaint Zealot Yellow, followed by reestablishing the highlights and edges with Sun Yellow and a little Vallejo Game Color Moon Yellow. The tip of the beak was painted with Pro Acryl Brown Grey, then highlighted with Brown Grey mixed with Bold Titanium White. 

I very very carefully airbrushed a little Army Painter Speedpaint Dark Wood on the back of the bird to heighten the depth of the feathers, then with a ton of caution, I drybrushed the feathers with a little Pro Acryl Light Umber, focusing the highlight towards the front.

Some superglue to join the bird’s legs to the arm piece, and she’s done!

I feel like I learned a lot from this piece; there are lots of different materials to practise rendering: skin, silk, wool, fur, and brass/gold. I think it all worked out very nicely.

title: I, for one, welcome Warhammer 40k's handicraft renaissance
content:
When Games Workshop announced pre-painted plastic terrain for Warhammer 40k, I was surprised at the technology, but not the luxury. We 40k fans have proven we'll pay through the nose, even for stuff that'll be out of date within months - so a tableful of good looking, zero effort terrain that'll last forever? Hot cakes.

When GW subsequently soft-revealed its prices on that painted terrain, I was even a bit shocked it wasn't more. But, as we dawdle through this sedate honeymoon period for Warhammer 40k 11th Edition, a quieter, pleasanter surprise has been GW's pointed nods toward the lost art of 'making stuff out of card for your games'.

Most recently, on Tuesday, Uncle Geedubs' Warhammer Community advertorial site announced free, downloadable, print and play versions of its official 11th edition terrain templates. Four different, themed art versions, in fact, designed to match jungle, snow, city, and, er, hellish worlds - and/or your basing theme and favorite Warhammer 40k factions - take your pick! They're meant to be printed onto A3 paper, cut out, and stuck to heavier card for use in your games. Yes, with scissors. Get an adult to help you.

A couple weeks before that, GW released a free PDF it'd made to go with the Kill Team: Exodite box set, providing detailed instructions, layouts, and to-the-millimeter measurements to make six different mystical Aeldari stoneworks, out of regular old cardboard. They look rad, too, especially the big, sweeping 'Nexoliths'. Will it be easy to construct something out of card that straddles the Eldar's subtle blend of ritual angles and organic curvature? Nah - but I sure as heck want to get my fingers sticky trying.

None of these little freebies are world-shatteringly thrilling on their own. They're not exactly big investments by the Great Beast of Nottingham, compared to the squillion megabucks it must have spent on terrain-painting machines (or the several squillion it expects to make back by selling crates of premade loveliness at over 340 bucks a pop).

But they're not nothing, either. They're minor indications - to me at least - that GW still recognizes the value of inspiring and encouraging scratch building and kitbashing. Our own Cat Bussell is right when she celebrates the "simple joy of building a mysterious space elf monolith out of what would otherwise be recycling". It's good to know that, at least from time to time, GW celebrates it too.

You know what, it's made me think Wargamer should make some print and play, cutout terrain templates too! What do you think, should we do it? Come join the Wargamer Discord community and let me know which you'd want to see.

title: [40K] Aeldari Exodites: The Tabletop Battles Hot Take
content:
Ahead of the release of the Kill Team: Exodite set this weekend, the full details of using Exodites in 40K (crucially including points costs) have been added to the Warhammer 40K app, so we can now take a look at how they might fit into Aeldari armies in the 41st Millennium.

The painted Exodites in this article are from a review copy provided to us by Games Workshop. Check out our Model Review for details of how building and painting them went!

Credit: Sky Serpent

General Rules

All the Exodites, both Characters and regulars, share quite a few common attributes. All their profiles are nearly identical - they're all M10" Mounted Mobile units, and defensively they're T5 with 4W (which is good), but flimsily armoured at only a 4+ with no invulnerable save. They're all OC2, and all except the Clanblade are Ld7+ (the noble leader gets 6+). They also all have an Extra Attacks offensive melee profile from their steeds, which is a respectable 3A WS3+ S5 AP-1, which doesn't light up the world, but combines with their regular output to let them really bully most other chaff.

All the Exodites also have the Aeldari Battle Focus army rule, providing them with extra speed and/or movement tricks, and crucially all have the Asuryani faction keyword, which ensures they're compatible with Stratagems and Enhancements from the Codex that care about this. That's especially relevant for the Warhost and Windrider Host Detachments, but has a few other niche benefits like the Stonesinger activating Seer Council Stratagems, and the units working fully with Ynnari.

The Units

Dragon Knights

Your regular Exodite squad is Dragon Knights, which come as either three models for 90pts or six for 180pts, with the standard statlines above.

Exodites are famous for fighting with laser lances, and those are on show here, each model getting a 3A WS3+ S6 AP-2 D3 Lance melee profile on top of their dragon's claws, and also one close range shot at S6 AP-2 D3. For shooting, each also packs a solar carbine, which is not too shabby - 18" 2A BS3+ S4 AP0 D1 with Rapid Fire 2 giving a decent amount of shots at close range if they need to clear out a cheap screen.

Their unit ability leans into being hard to pin down, with the unit being able to fall-back, shoot and charge freely. They can also fight in a fairly loose melee formation thanks to the Agile Reach ability, which means that as long as the unit is engaged with a foe, models in the unit that are within 3" of the enemy get to fight rather than just 2".

Finally, for each three models in the squad they can take two Drakolithe tokens. When an enemy ends a move either within 8" of an unengaged unit of Dragon Knights, or engaged with them, you can spend one token to try and deal them a Mortal Wound on a 3+. It's a neat extra bonus, and don't forget that Pile Ins are a move, so if an opponent charges you then piles in, you can blow multiple tokens in quick succession.

How does this stack up? At baseline, this unit is pretty deadly for 90pts, and although the lack of an invulnerable save is painful, just being T5 with 4W each makes them quite a bit sturdier than some other things in the roster that you can spend this many points on, though obviously with a larger footprint. Like a lot of Aeldari units, they do suffer significantly from the faction being desperately short of re-rolls, which means they have to be quite judicious about picking targets, and can sometimes just whiff.

By themselves, I think these are at least worth a look in Warhost, Windrider Host and Devoted of Ynnead. As a Recon Detachment, Warhost is pretty happy to spend 90pts on a reasonably fast unit that can expect to charge something and do meaningful damage before going down. You can also use Lightning Fast Reactions to improve their durability, and boosted Battle Focus can either help get where they're needed, or get them out of trouble. In Ynnari, meanwhile, being a T5 Mounted unit is really good with Macabre Resilience, as this is unconditional -1 to Wound, so can badly blank anything that tries to handle these with S4 stuff, and Ynnari are also generically happy to have a 90pts brawler unit rolling around, plus fast OC6 to tip an objective against 5-model chaff when playing Priority Assets.

Both of those pale against the biggest game in town, which is obviously Windrider Host. Everything in this Detachment only cares about MOUNTED, not MOUNTED FLY, so these work with pretty much everything, including freely leaping back into reserves, moving after killing something, Advancing and Charging and (most importantly) getting a 4+ Invulnerable Save against shooting. They compete with Shining Spears for a slot, but it feels like there's a real argument for taking some of each, especially as the Exodite lances are S6 rather than S5, so hit better into Gravis-style Infantry. A full six-model unit is also easier to position than an equivalent Shining Spear squad thanks to the large round bases on the latter, particularly with Agile Reach to help. Definite game here for both sizes of unit.

These three Detachments are also where you might choose to boost your squad with some added Characters, and you get two options for this.

Clanblade

Credit: Dan "Swiftblade" Richardson

The Clanblade is a force multiplier for Dragon Knights who also diversifies their melee output a bit. As a Leader, he gives the whole unit Sustained Hits 1 in melee, which is very nasty on a squad's laser lances. He also leans into them being used as disruptive bully pieces via the Cornered Prey rule, which means any unit falling back from them has to use Desperate Escape, with all the risks inherent in that. Unlike some rules like this, it does affect enemy Monsters and Vehicles, so can be particularly good for pinning down enemy hulls.

The Clanblade also brings their own weapons to the fight, swinging with moonblades that hit at 5A WS2+ S4 AP-2 D2, and adding reliability via both Lethal Hits and Twin-Linked. There's a little bit of tension here with this being a pretty pure anti-Infantry profile where the rest of the unit can flex between most targets, but the abilities smooth that out so that the Clanblade won't do nothing into a hull, and adding Sustained to the rest of the unit's lances there seems great.

As a Character, the Clanblade can also take Enhancements, and there are some great options in both Windrider and Warhost. Windrider's best options are either Firstdrawn Blade, providing Scouts 9" at a bargain price, or Mirage Field to give the unit a permanent -1 to Hit, which is tempting if you're going for a full squad. Warhost, meanwhile, adds the Gift of Foresight enhancement, providing a free use of Command re-roll each Battle Round, which these seem better suited for than most places you can currently put that.

The Clanblade comes in at 70pts, so a basic squad with one runs you 160pts which seems OK as a counter-charge threat with enough reach to go out and press the attack when needed, but might fall in that awkward in-between spot where they're a little too pricy for a throwaway unit (whereas three regulars alone are cheap), but not consistently deadly enough that they make the cut over something spicier. They also need a pretty big staging spot, which are somewhat at a premium on the current maps. In Windrider Host I don't think that matters and you're very happy just taking a squad, and I think they could work in Warhost, but that you may end up just taking a bare bones squad and calling it a day.

Sky Serpent: I really like the Clanblade but it feels to me that if it’s a choice of adding one to a unit or more Dragon Knights, I’d find the 20pts and just go for a bigger unit. The Clanblade leading a Dinosaur Deathstar is an enticing prospect but likely a little costly too, just go all in with some sprinkling of Windrider Host enhancements that Wings suggested above.

Stonesinger

Credit: Sky Serpent

Your other Character option is the Stonesinger, who is a Support for the Knights. This means you can't take them alone (and you low key might otherwise), but can choose to add both Characters to a squad if you so choose.

Whether you would actually do that is a little uncertain, as the Stonesinger pulls in a quite different direction than the rest of the setup here, being focused on ranged attacks. The ranged attacks they have are none too shabby, supplementing the regular solar carbine with a psychic attack for hitting Monsters/Vehicles and an acid-spit Torrent attack for elite infantry. The Psychic attack is three shots at BS3+ S4 AP-2 D3 with Anti-Monster/Vehicle 3+, while the torrent is anti-Non Monster/Vehicle 3+, and has 3 shots with Blast at S3, and AP-2 D2. Both of these are good profiles, even if they want to target completely separate things, and increase the unit's multi-phase threat quite considerably (and the spit is decent enough for Overwatch). In melee they're a bit weaker than the rest of the squad, swinging with their staff, which does get to be anti-Non Monster/Vehicle 2+, but only gets three attacks at AP-1 D1.

The last trick they have up their sleeve is a Psychic ability that you trigger at the end of your Fight Phase as long as the unit isn't Battle-shocked. If you do, you roll a d6, and on anything except a 1, pick a visible enemy Monster/Vehicle (not Titanic) to be Ensnared until your next turn, getting -2" to move (this does not stack with Pinned from Night Spinners). This is OK, but has some risks to it - if you roll a 1, your unit gets Battle-shocked, and more generally if you can see an enemy Vehicle they can see you, which is often ominous for this unit's survival prospects.

The Stonesinger is slightly cheaper than the Clanblade at 60pts, so if you desperately need to squeeze an Enhancement on, they're a slightly cheaper route to that. They do also diversify the unit's capabilities a fair bit, as in some situations they'll be able to do some meaningful damage without rocking into melee. That might make a unit with one interesting in Warhost, where you can be more cagey with how you use them, but I think the biggest draw for the Stonesinger is that it switches on a bunch of stuff in Seer Council. They're a pretty good place to put the Torc of Morai-Heg, since they'll generally be close to the action, and that also makes them excellent for triggering Isha's Fury or Presentiment of Dread. If you really want to ruin the day of Thousand Sons specifically, you could also take Runes of Warding here.

I think on balance, outside of Seer Council, I'm more interested in taking a Clanblade than a Stonesinger, but being cheaper does create some appeal. Seer Council is also the main place I'd be especially excited about a unit with both - this can fill the dual purpose of providing a moderately sturdy counter-charge piece and moving a large-based Psyker into position on a key turn, particularly if you add the Torc.

Leystalker

Credit: Sky Serpent

Last, but certainly not least, is the Leystalker. They have the standard profile for the units, but are much harder to pin down and deal with thanks to having Lone Operative. Supplementing this with Scout 9" makes these ideal position pieces, and particularly good in Recon or Priority Assets plans.

They also have a decently nasty shooting attack, firing two shots at 36" with BS2+ S6 AP-2 D3 with Precision, and Devastating Wounds against non-Vehicle/Monster targets. Any non-Vehicle/Monster that they hit also has to take a Battle-shock test at -1. In exchange for this their melee is pretty paltry, but they do get a couple of Drakolithes (that work the same as for the Knights) to take a few foes with them if charged.

This package runs you 80pts, and that's pretty great. They're slightly pricier than the Death Jester as a Lone Operative, but they have some upsides that recommend them (and you can also just take both, and you can't normally take more than one Jester). The large base makes them better for screening, and OC2 on a Lone Operative is quite rare, and lets them trump single models touching a point. They're also the first Asuryani Lone Operative, which gives them some interesting Enhancement options. Warhost shines here - they're another place you'd be perfectly happy to put Gift of Foresight to increase their reliability, and if you're willing to go spendy, they're one of the best places for the Phoenix Gem. There's also a surprisingly relevant option in Guardian Battlehost, with Craftworld's Champion giving them OC5. That's extremely good on a single model, and can really help smooth over the Primary at key points, or stopping enemy attempts to flip your expansion.

The Leystalker seems near certain to see play, as they're just a good unit. Like the others, Windrider host boosts them even further, as being able to pull them into Reserves adds even more value, but I can see taking the Leystalker in almost any Aeldari list.

Wrap Up

Some much-needed Aeldari reinforcements here, and honestly pretty fairly priced - there are certainly places I'm keen to try these, without any of them screaming out that they're busted. Good stuff.

Sky Serpent: I think the release of a subfaction that many Eldar enjoyers have been pining for for decades is so incredibly exciting and these datasheets are a great start. You’ll likely see many players start Aeldari armies just to field these models and the next puzzle to solve will be what to field alongside them; dino fingers crossed for a 1DP Exodite Detachment in a future update. title: Two years into the world's most complicated board game, masochist gamers "still don't understand what the camels do"
content:
Widely regarded as the most complicated board game ever made, The Campaign for North Africa tries to simulate WW2's North African theater in as granular fashion as possible, with rules for everything from water spillage and evaporation to convoy truck breakdowns.

As a result, this 1978 title by Simulations Publications Inc is about as complicated to run as a real life war. Since the campaign it depicts took place between 1940 and 1943, it also takes at least as long to finish.

Infamous for its "pasta rule" which requires Italian troops to use more water supplies so they can cook spaghetti, The Campaign for North Africa is either a work of mad genius or a really unusual torture device. The game boasts a whopping 1,500 hours of play time (and you know designers always underestimate these things). The game's rules recommend you play with ten people, five to a side, with each person taking control of  just one facet of the conflict, so that their brains don't explode. I'm paraphrasing slightly.

Like horror movie characters ignoring clear and obvious warnings, a pair of friends, Andy and James, have paid no heed to this suggestion. They are trying to complete The Campaign for North Africa all by themselves, documenting the process in podcast form. 20 months and 88 episodes after this folly began, they are finally done with the six-turn practice scenario, and are ready for the entire 111-turn war. Sharing their thoughts on the game via Reddit, they say "The work:fun ratio of The Campaign For North Africa is askew".

Only getting together once a week for a few hours, the gamers were forced to come up with several nifty time-saving measures. These included magnetizing the maps and each game piece, to make setup the work of minutes rather than hours, and creating their own searchable PDF-version of the rules to speed up rule checking. They also used digital spreadsheets with automated calculations, to help with the immense amount of book-keeping The Campaign For North Africa demands from its victims. Ahem, I mean players.

Their recent longform Reddit post about the experience is a lot of fun to read. It's full of gems like: "We still don't understand what the camels do". Sessions where all the two did was move trucks around in preparation for later fun, are described as low points of the gameplay, though they do say they enjoyed the dogfights during the air phase.

Going into more depth, the post describes The Campaign For North Africa as a "beautiful simulation of the uncaringly mundane slog of war command" but concludes that "unless you thoroughly enjoy the granular detail of breakdown of vehicles, consumption of fuel, updating of cohesion levels and CPA constantly, you'll likely not enjoy playing this game for very long."

And it seems no one has played it for very long, because although the game's creators told Kotaku they expect someone has finished it, zero complete playthroughs have actually ever been recorded. Could this be the first?

The duo's website 'War With a Mate' gives little explanation for why Andy and James embarked on this adventure, besides running out of conversation topics after ten years of friendship. Apparently they aren't experienced wargamers, citing Risk as the only game like this they've ever played. Their website says they're going to continue out of sheer bloody-minded stubbornness, though, even if it takes the rest of their mortal lives.

I don't know whether I should salute, or slowly back away around a corner and run like hell.

title: Gundam Slingers: Getting Started with the Gundam Card Game
content:
The world of trading card games is currently going through something of a boom period, with lots of new games and ideas vying for your hard earned attention and money; while Magic the Gathering and Pokémon still dominate much of the conversation, there are a lot of other games out there that have engaging mechanics, competitive play, and unique ways of interacting with the expectations of a card game. Quite a few of these games come from the same place lately: Bandai, a company that has access to numerous anime based IPs and the ability to leverage them into games, such as Digimon, One Piece, Dragon Ball Z, Gundam, and the newly announced Naruto card game. Some of these games are beholden to the “investor” market, namely One Piece, but almost all of them are quite alive and have a thriving competitive scene; personally, we’re pretty fond of Gundams here at Tabletop Battles, and my recent ability to interact with and learn the Gundam Card Game made it an easy fit to bring to our site. Today, I want to do something of a combination review and Getting Started piece, going over what makes the game tick, how it is unique and fun, why you might want to take a look at it, and then how to best start your journey into Gundam Card Game play!

A Newtype of Game

Depending on your familiarity with trading card games, the Gundam Card Game can be remarkably easy to pick up once the basics are explained, but even with total unfamiliarity with card games in general, the system at play here is fairly simple, making it quite beginner friendly and having the “low skill floor, high skill ceiling” type of gameplay that can make a card game fun to continue coming back to. In Gundam, each player has a deck of 50 cards, 10 Resources, and a starting Base card that comprises what they have to work with. The Resource mechanic is very similar to other Bandai card games, in that it is a separate pile of cards that allow you to pay for the things you’d like to do in the game; they also are somewhat similar to Lands in Magic, although Lands don’t exist outside of their main deck and the drawing (or not drawing) of them can become part of the fun (or frustration) of Magic’s playstyle.

The general layout of a Gundam Card Game match: Your base and shields to the left, the action area in the top middle, your resources and resource deck at the bottom, your deck top right, and trash to the bottom right.

Within a deck, players also have a few different card types: Mobile Suits, which make up the units you’ll use to attack and defend with, Pilots, who can be equipped to Mobile Suits and provide various benefits and abilities when they do so, Command cards, which generally feature immediate actions such as dealing direct damage, drawing cards, searching your deck, or more, and Base cards, which can be played to replace your starting Base and provide you with some extra defense. Decks have pretty basic construction rules, with a 50 card limit that can include 2 colors and 4 types of the same card (there are some more restrictions with the most recent Banned and Restricted changes, but that’s a little more granular than an initial overview can get into). Once you have a deck and have started playing, players place 6 cards from the tops of their decks next to their Base, creating a set of Shields. Again, these are very similar set up to games like One Piece, and functions very much the same way: when you take damage to your Shield, you flip the card over; if it has a Burst action, the card does what it says, and otherwise, it goes to your Trash. Once you’ve lost your Base and all 6 Shields, any damage dealt to “you” ends the game.

What we're all here for: Gundams. Mobile suits and some other vehicles make up the Units in GGC.

Gameflow is fairly quick and easy to get into: players draw 5, and then may Mulligan once. Play starts once a first player is determined, and players have “levels” that determine what cards they can play. Player 1 will always start at level 1, and level is decided by your Resources available; Player 2 is given an “EX Resource” card that, when used, is expended, but also functions as a level, meaning that going 2nd is not inherently a death sentence and that the extra level can help the second player stay on tempo. Level determines what cards you can play, but Resources then determine what you can pay for, which gave us nice flexibility during our turns during playtesting.

Pilots like Machu attach to Units, and can even allow them to act the same turn you play them if they're Linked.

Units are unable to attack upon being deployed (unless the card says otherwise, of course), so this can also help with turn order play and not feeling bad about going second; units also have choices of what they wish to attack, being able to choose between a player’s Base or Shield, or Rested units; in playing, we really enjoyed the choices available, and some cards even make it lucrative to trade Units in combat with various effects, rather than simply ignoring each other and seeing who can slam into the other’s Shields faster.  During our playtesting, going full out hard aggro against Shields also didn’t often pay off, instead resulting in leaving the over aggressive player often at a disadvantage, generally running out of steam quickly and having very little ability to recover.

Command cards such as Overflowing Affection allow you to draw cards, do direct damage, or other effects, and help break up the flow of the game.

That, perhaps, is what we found most enjoyable with the game: Tempo. Playing smart and playing in a timing focused method resulted in deeper gameplay and much more interesting matches, but it also tended to make our games fairly evenly matched. The current competitive meta does tend to focus heavily on aggression, but generally through decks that enable aggressive play and have cards that then allow that aggression to pay off. There are some various styles of play, too, often designated by keywords; for example, Gundam GQuuuuuuX tends to be tagged “Clan”, and feature numerous cards that search for, play off of, or work together with that keyword. This also extends to Pilots, who have the ability to “Link” with specific Units. Although Pilots can be attached to any Unit, when a Pilot is attached to a Unit that they are “Linked” to, they enable that Unit to activate immediately, as well as sometimes giving them specific powers or abilities.

If you're interested in trying the multiplayer variants, this starter deck is a good place to look for that, but can be a little odd otherwise.

Overall, games of Gundam lasted about 25~35 minutes in our play, and generally rewarded 2 out of 3 sessions to get a good sense of variability and feeling while playing. We also tended to have fairly equal and tied wins and losses, and the game generally feels very well balanced. We haven’t had much of a chance to try the other play variants, a 2-4 player free for all or 2 v 2 team battles, but one interesting aspect of this mode is that a set, Eternal Nexus, even features specific and unique cards that make those game modes more interesting and provide cards that work differently when there are multiple players at the table; in an upcoming article, we’ll take a look at these modes in more detail, as knowing what you can do with a game is always a helpful way to inform whether it is right for your table; currently, we appreciate that it exists, but have no hands-on experience yet!

How to get Started with Gundam

There are a few options available to get in to the game at the moment: buying Starter decks, or buying Singles. I’ve mentioned in previous articles that I’m not always the biggest fan of having to rely on Singles as the best way to get into a game, mostly just in that it can sometimes remove the sense of community or camaraderie from a game that you can’t “buy” easily, but like many card games right now, Gundam is going through a bit of growing pains with the “investment” market trying to make the game a new cash cow. The recent release of Freedom Ascension, the newest set, saw this as booster boxes and a Deck Building Kit sell out almost immediately and start to be resold at above average prices on the market. In general, though, Gundam is a very affordable game that benefits from the fact that “playable” cards are not the cards “collectors” want, and so to play the game, decks will often run around 40-60 dollars, with some being slightly more if they are the current top meta decks in the game.

There are a few more Starters coming in September, and some older Starters that were packed with Gundam Assemble kits, but right now you might be best off looking for some variety of these to get started with.

However, one good note here is that the starter decks available for the game all provide very balanced and fun ways to get into the game, and finding them tends to be fairly easy compared to buying the cards in bulk via booster boxes. Clan Unity, Iron Bloom, Flash of Radiance and Celestial Drive are the 4 current decks that you’ll often see floating around, and we were able to pick them up and test them out during our initial learning phase of the game. They all tend to focus on specific keywords, which does bring us to one vexing aspect of the game: If you’re looking to play a specific Gundam series, you’ll have to figure out what their keyword is, and then figuring out what card work best with those. For example, Clan tends to be so far attached only to GQuuuuuuX, meaning that Cland decks really only want GQuuuuuuX focused cards. But most competitive decks tend to focus on deck synergy over Gundam series, and there are some choices to be made about playing the game for fun and playing the game competitively; this is often the odd part of licensed games, so if you want to play as your favorite Gundam series, you’ll need to figure out the deck that correlates to them, or otherwise, enjoy playing within the various Gundam Universes by finding a deck you like to play instead.

Destiny Ignition gives you 22 extra cards to start customizing and deck building in the box, which is great for practice and learning.

There are two other Starter Deck options around: Destiny Ignition, which is an interesting deck that allows a player to take the cards provided and customize the deck with a provided amount of extra cards; I actually really enjoyed this product and would love to see more things like this in other card games, because it provides a pre-made deck that then immediately gives the player access to new ideas and tinker with the deck. The Deck Builder Box from Freedom Ascension works very similar, providing players with a set of different color options and then allowing them to build a deck from that; if you can find that box for a price close to MSRP, it can be the best box to start with. The last current starter deck, Generation Pulse, features cards from Eternal Nexus that makes the deck ready to be used for Multiplayer Variants, and while it does work for 1 on 1 play, it did feel slightly lopsided against decks that were specifically made to play 1v1.

Sadly this box can be difficult to find at the moment, but it contains a slew of reprinted staple cards from the original starters, and allows a player to build a custom deck from what's included. If you can find it for around MSRP, it is absolutely the best place to start.

Otherwise, your best bet is to look up various decks Bandai notes for competitive play wins, and try to build one off of those from singles. Ironically, this isn’t exactly that much more expensive than buying in with starter decks, as they tend to run 20 dollars for most basic decks, 40 for Destiny Ignition, and the Build Box tends to float around 60~80 dollars at fair market values. A single deck made of singles bought off the market will run around 40~80 dollars at max, especially if you avoid premium alternate art cards, so consider what you’d like to play and how you’d like to get into it; it may also be worth seeing if your LGS carries the game and has a community, as I was able to source some singles from there as well as trade with players and get some access to staples like extra Resources and commonly used common cards far below what I’d normally pay for it with taxes and shipping.

What’s Next?

Shout out to Calcifercurse, who made this amazing playmat! Not sponsored, we just loved the design and its what we use to play on now.

Hopefully, our primer has given you some encouragement to try out Gundam Card Game and see if it is for you; we think it is a great game and has a lot of playability and life, and since it just celebrated a year on the market in English, there is likely a lot more to come from Bandai as there are 4 new Starter Decks and booster sets on the horizon. The tie-ins with Gundam Assemble also hint at the fact that Gundam has a lot of room to grow from here; in our next feature, we’ll be taking the Starter Decks and discussing how to build off of them, their strengths and weaknesses, and how various deck synergies, strategies, and more can work for players looking to get started with the game. We hope you’ll enjoy it with us as we move towards more discussions of competitive deckbuilding and the world of the Gundam Card Game!

title: Games from the Crypt #19 - Games of the Rings, Book 1
content:
I’m currently in the throes of Middle-Earth mania, going so far as to re-read The Silmarillion and conducting an annual re-watch of Peter Jackson films. Which gets pretty grueling once you hit the Hobbit films, which are mostly about weird beards and falling. Naturally, while I’m waiting hours and hours for The Hobbit series to tell a 2 hour tops story, my mind wanders to the Game Crypt and the many great Lord of the Rings and Hobbit games that have come and gone over the years. So over the next couple of columns, I’ll be taking a look at some of my favorites.

First things first, I know for many readers, the classic War of the Ring immediately springs to mind. It’s definitely a great game, but it’s also one that I think has been covered sufficiently. Hell I even wrote a two part strategy guide for it back in the day for the print edition of Games International magazine. And I don’t write strategy guides! It’s also sort of emerged as the de facto, evergreen Tolkien game over the 20+ years (are you kidding me) that it’s been around, so it hardly needs an exhumation from the crypt. Likewise, the recently popular Lord of the Rings: Fate of the Fellowship and Fantasy Flight’s Journeys in Middle-Earth aren’t really eligible for a crypt-kick. And neither is Love Letter: The Hobbit. For Manwe’s sake!

But a Tolkien game that could use some fresh air, I think, is what I still believe to be the finest game set in Middle-Earth to date. 26 years ago the master of modern game design, Reiner Knizia, put out a Lord of the Rings board game that remains the best example of Tolkien’s themes, concepts, and narrative translated to the tabletop medium and with amazing John Howe artwork to boot. Sure, War of the Ring captures the martial thrill of the titular conflict, but it isn’t really about the things that the story is actually about- unexpected courage, overcoming impossible odds, avoiding corruption, lots of walking, and friendship. Indeed, many detractors of this game decry it as “that game where you play friendship cards.” And in fact, you actually do. But this ambitious game aims to tell the entire story of The Lord of the Rings from Bilbo’s birthday all the way to the slam dunk in Mount Doom.

This is tricky business for a designer - to convey the same narrative beats, events and sequences while still affording players the agency to shape outcomes and to encounter fail states that prematurely end the narrative. But Knizia absolutely was up to the task and he did some quite innovative things in terms of design. One was to make the game completely cooperative at a time when co-op games were extremely rare- each player represented one of the Hobbits from the story (along with the barely mentioned Fatty Bolger to allow a fifth player) working together and sharing resources to overcome challenges. Another innovation was to frame the narrative across multiple boards depicting key events and sections of the book so that the path the game progresses along quite literally moves the player through the story with checkpoints along the way to bring in other characters, subplots, and “timed” events. And another still was separating the main board from a smaller board depicting not only the overall story progression but also each Hobbit’s relative corruption- and the increasing proximity of Sauron to them.

Mechanically it’s quite simple and it’s sort of, really, a card game with some randomly drawn resource tiles available to players. All players are represented on the story boards by a single piece on three separate tracks, which are moved when cards are played matching the right symbols, sometimes triggering events or challenges that must be either singularly or collectively overcome by paying the right resources. The game is chockablock full of single-use, one-time-only cards representing everything from Lembas bread to Glimmering that create impactful decision points - do you spend this now, or wait until later? The Hobbits also have a set of Gandalf cards that can save their bacon in a pinch but there again, it’s always a question if it’s worth it to spend now or save for later. Failing tasks- or using the Ring to avoid negative consequences- incurs corruption. And if Sauron and a Hobbit ever wind up in the same corruption space, the Hobbit is eliminated.

One of the most genius aspects of this game is this concept of choosing corruption to avoid potentially worse outcomes. The Ring tempts, just like it does in the book. And as the game progresses along the story tracks, resources become more and more scarce. Hand sizes dwindle. By the time the party makes it to Mordor, it becomes absolutely grueling with every turn feeling like you are just scraping by. It is exactly the right tone, and in the way the game is paced it once again demonstrates how Knizia, more than any other designer who has ever worked in tabletop gaming, understands what theme actually is and how gameplay and mechanics interact alchemically to create meaning.

Of all the co-op games that have come along since this game, I still think this is the best one ever published with or without the Lord of the Rings livery. “Beating” it feels like a genuine accomplishment, and the feeling that you’ve survived the entire journey is truly rewarding. It is a difficult game but there are some tweaks that make it easier. Don’t be tempted to use them.

The game was quite successful back in the day and three expansions were released. I think the Friends and Foes expansion is actually essential- it expands the theme of conflict and puts a line of enemy cards on the table that must be defeated in addition to the tasks on the board. It ratchets up the tension quite a bit, but there are rewards for defeating the Uruk-Hai, Crebain, Wargs, and other baddies that file out of the Black Gate. It also added a third double-sided story board with Bree and Isengard to incorporate more of the story. The common thinking at the time was that if you got the base game, you bought Friends and Foes at the same time.

The Sauron expansion was also quite great. The best thing to come out of it is a velvet Eye of Sauron bag to put the resource tiles in along with a great set of Sauron action tiles to make drawing resources a risky proposition as they generally do really bad things and make The Lidless Eye more of a direct threat. There was also a Black Rider figure added to the Corruption track- when activated, he issues forth from the last space on the corruption track and if he meets up with the Ringbearer, he hauls it back to Mordor to end the game in an L for the Free Peoples of Middle-Earth. Less successful in this package was a set of rules that make it possible for someone to play Sauron. It sucked, to be blunt, and I think I maybe played this way twice before never doing it again.

Battlefields was released a few years later and it was barely in print - today, it commands prices of $200 and up. I had it, and played it a few times, and to this day I find it compelling and intriguing from a design perspective, but it also feels somewhat experimental and detached from the core game. It added three double-sided battle boards that depicted the battles and larger conflicts of the story in greater detail. It did create a sense of parallel action and resolution as is appropriate, but mechanically it felt somewhat overwrought and I’m not sure that the flowchart-like boards really captured the right tone. What’s more, they seemed to make an already very difficult game even more difficult, and I never felt like the increase in challenge was welcome.

These days, this incredible game is out of print despite selling close to a million copies worldwide, having last been published in 2020 anniversary edition not compatible with any of the expansions - which is a tremendous loss as this is one of the best adventure games of all time, and the best LOTR game ever. There’s not even an online implementation anywhere, so those seeking to enjoy it today are going to have to go to the secondary market and shell out the bucks- at least if you want to play with the expansions.

title: MTG card that's perfect for treasure decks sees a 725% price spike
content:
The Magic: The Gathering card Rain of Riches is spiking hard right now. This card has appeared in a number of Commander decks, but the cheapest version from Bloomburrow has risen from $1.30 to $10.75 in the past two weeks - a rise of 726%. The reason for this particular spike is no secret. It's all to do with The Hobbit cards, every last one of which was recently revealed.

Rain of Riches is a five-mana card for treasure decks that makes you a couple of treasures, then gives the first spell you cast with treasure each turn the cascade keyword. That can mean a ton of free spells for devoted treasure decks, especially if you're running plenty of instant speed cards and can activate this ability on your opponents' turns.

The Hobbit set has a bit of a treasures theme, with close to 20 cards that mention the token type in their rules text, including some really powerful ones like Gleaming Splendor. In particular, there are some powerful treasure synergies based around Smaug and the dwarves - arguably the two most attractive elements of this entire MTG set.

On the dwarf side, the card most relevant to this spike is Thorin, King of Durin's Folk, who makes treasure whenever a dwarf enters and buffs them all up in the process. Assuming you have a lot of dwarves in your Thorin deck (if you don't, maybe go back and build it again) you'll often end up making replacement treasures with the creatures you cascade into, which is a tasty bit of synergy.

The deluge of dwarves has also increased interest in Magda, a cEDH level commander that makes treasure whenever you tap a dwarf. It probably isn't the best place for it, but I could easily see Rain of Riches being bundled into a more casual version of this deck.

Then there's the Smaug cards, and all three of them (the Impenetrable, the Magnificent, and Wicked Worm) work with treasure - they also synergize pretty well with each other. While the other two contribute, Smaug the Magnificent is the most popular and most relevant here, as it wants to build up a critical mass of treasure to blast opponents for lethal damage.

Though Rain of Riches doesn't do that much treasure-making on its own, if your entire deck is singlehandedly designed around making as treasure as possible then it will play a great role in speeding up your gameplan, fetching you Reaver Cleavers and Xorns that can generate more cash money.

With spoiler season for The Hobbit now at a close, I'm expecting more price spikes created by these cards over the next few weeks. We'll keep our eyes open, and let you know what we find.

title: [40k] Competitive Innovations in 11th: Rolling Need pt.1
content:
Welcome to Competitive Innovations, our weekly feature for a number of game lines across the tabletop wargame space. Each week our army list and tactics experts canvass the top tournaments for their game of specialty, looking at the week’s top match-ups and how they played out on the tabletop to let you know what’s hot, what’s not, and what might be coming next as the competitive meta evolves year-round.

Welcome back to Competitive Innovations in 11th edition! Your regular host, James "One_Wing" Grover is out this week. And so is Tom "lowest of men" Lowman. So instead you just get me! I'd like to think I bring a certain amount of charm and wit to the table that they don't, at the expense of any sense of "class" or "propriety."

This weekend's events represents the first weekend of games following the July 2026 balance update, and hoo boy did that one do a number on the competitive landscape. It feels like Purge the Foe disappeared overnight as an option, as it's no longer really attached to any good Detachments and they removed it from almost every 1 DP Detachment in the game. What we're left with is a weekend in which there were zero winning lists running either Purge the Foe or Disruption. This feels like a bad sign - we've gone from having four viable Dispositions to three. I personally played the Take and Hold mirror in all three of my day one games at the Lone Star Open.

Looking at the data from competitive events over the past four weeks shows off this particular trend. Namely, that players have (accurately) figured out that Disruption just kind of sucks, and now that Purge is really hard to get in a good list, the disposition now makes up about 1/6 of the field, while Take and Hold and Priority Assets lists now make up more than 60%, each accounting for about 31% of the field.

This ultimately highlights the problems with the July balance update, and ultimately the detachment/disposition system as it currently stands: Dispositions are very strongly tied to the strength of the Detachments they're paired with. Players aren't going to take a bad detachment for a good disposition, but they can play around a mediocre disposition if the detachment is particularly strong (as long as it's not Disruption, it seems). This means that making Purge unavailable to good detachments means that it's just not an option for most of the game's armies when played competitively. Rather than Purge being fixed, it's just now not showing up, and the result is that players get in a lot of mirrors with Take & Hold or Priority Assets.

So if you're a competitive player looking to practice for a singles event, my advice is to get comfortable playing against Take and Hold and Priority Assets. If you can shore up your matchup into those dispositions, you'll likely knock out more than half the games you play at an event.

I asked Mike for his thoughts on the list and his matchup in the final round against Drukhari, and this is what he had to say:

Mike: The Purge The Foe vs Recon matchup goes one of two ways. The first is that the Purge player plays cagey and the Recon player is able to play defensively. That’s a boring, drawish game.

The second option is that the Purge The Foe player shoves all-in and tries to table the Recon player. That’s a fun, quick game. That game also happens to be heavily Purge The Foe favored, especially if the Purge player goes first. That means the Purge player has 2 turns to try to kill as much as they can before the Recon player can even start doing their action to start scoring Primary.

His Drukhari list was built around being uninteractive, with 2 units of Scourges that could fire and fade back to safety, and the ability for high-damage melee bricks to jump out of a transport, delete a unit, and then jump back into a transport. I didn’t want to play a 5-round game of attrition vs a strong player with a list that would win an attrition war. That further incentivized me to rush him early.

Andrew is a really strong player (and a friend), but when I got to the table, I knew what I had to do.

All of that is to say that I deployed on the line, literally advanced everything turn 1, used the Cavalcade Of Chaos stratagem to bring in my Bloodcrushers turn 1, and prepared to go all-in turn 2 after killing some screens. Andrew took a decent chunk out of my army and I lost around ~10 Bloodcrushers, but by turn 2 I was able to charge my entire army in and kill most of his real damage dealers. Andrew smartly basically left his deployment zone and started playing the flanks to scrap for points, but the Blood Legion all-in on turn 2 took out enough of the fragile elves that they could never regain any momentum. It’s always fun playing Andrew (or any of my teammates on the Mile High Militarum) but this matchup definitely felt Blood Legion favored. All I had to do was avoid any glaring mistakes (which isn’t guaranteed by the sixth round of a GT!) and execute the gameplan to end up on the podium.

Thanks, Mike and congrats on the podium finish.

title: The 8 biggest chase cards in Pokémon Delta Reign
content:
Though we still have several months to wait for Pokémon Delta Reign, the set's Japanese equivalent, Storm Emeralda, recently hit store shelves, giving us a solid picture of what's coming in the English release. With the smallest main set in a couple of decades, it's not all that surprising that there are fewer big hitters than a juggernaut like Ascended Heroes, but there's still plenty to look forward to. Here you'll find a list of the best Delta Reign chase cards you should hope to collect when the set comes out on November 6.

While the English language cards and set list haven't been officially confirmed, it's become pretty straightforward to draw a 1:1 comparison between English and Japanese sets these days. We'll keep an eye out though. If a surprise new batch of SIRs is plonked into Delta Reign, we'll add the best ones here.

Kecleon

The clear standout when it comes to Delta Reign Illustration Rares that aren't legendary Pokémon, I don't think anyone could've predicted Kecleon would be one of the chase cards of the Rayquaza set. Despite playing a role as a hidden path blocker in the Hoenn games and an absurdly overpowered shopkeeper in Mystery Dungeon, Kecleon is one of the most often forgotten Gen 3 Pokémon. With no evolution, regional form, megas, or anything else to draw recent attention to him, you could say Kecleon is completely camouflaged.

There's no disguising yourself against that background, and this Kecleon has wisely decided not to even try.

Mega Golisopod ex

Mega Golisopod got a fairly standard Special Illustration Rare here, but it's one that makes this overgrown arthropod look particularly beastly - just look at its eyes! This is the first Golisopod full art that actually shows the Pokémon in battling action, making it a worthy addition to any collection. I have to point out though, that the big claw in the foreground obscures the Mega Golisopod's belly, meaning we can't tell if it was drawn correctly.

Kyogre

While Kyogre and Groudon didn't get SIR cards in this set, presumably so as not to overshadow the big green noodle, their Illustration Rares are top notch. In fact, this may just be the best Kyogre card of all time, effortlessly showing the creature's immense power and connection with the ocean.

If you're building a binder, you might want to check out the Groudon IR from Paradox Rift. These two cards share an artist, making it perhaps a better counterpart to this Kyogre than Delta Reign's own Groudon card.

Groudon

Not that Delta Reign's Groudon is anything to be disappointed about. We got a big scary red lizard monster covered in lava - what's not to like?

Zinnia's Trust

Amidst the busyness of modern Pokémon art, it's nice to have a Special Illustration Rare that's a little calmer, a touch more serene. This depiction of the character Zinnia is wonderfully charming, with a great painterly style and a stunning backdrop, just hinting at the staggering height of the Sky Pillar.

Though she only shows up in the post-game, Zinnia is one of Omega Ruby and Alpha Sapphire's most memorable (and controversial) characters, and this supporter card depicts a pivotal moment in the plot, where she entrusts the fate of the world to you, the player.

Raikou ex

Oh damn. You better run. This Raikou is coming for you. With the Storm Emeralda packaging so heavily dominated by Rayquaza, it was actually a surprise to see Delta Reign had another legendary SIR - though certainly a welcome one.

Regular Raikou has taken somewhat of a backseat to Raging Bolt of late, but the standard storm beast returns here in style, looking downright dangerous. This card may actually rival the Rayquazas for the best in the set.

Mega Rayquaza ex Mega Hyper Rare

Though they're all a bit similar-looking, these golden 'Mega Hyper Rare' cards take a place on this list because they're so flipping rare. And… I must begrudgingly admit, they are pretty cool, as well. I guess.

Mega Rayquaza ex SIR

However, this is the gold Rayquaza I really want! The biggest and best card in the entire Delta Reign set is a surprisingly polarizing Special Illustration Rare for Rayquaza. While I've seen the gorgeous card getting its flowers from plenty of fans, others aren't so keen. It's possible fans might finally be tiring on the ultra-detailed backgrounds in these big hitter chase cards.

However, I don't think a small band of online naysayers are going to do anything to affect this card's price tag: it's undoubtedly destined to be the biggest chase. What do you think of the artwork here? Frankly, I find the color and texture work a little awe-inspiring, especially as this artist has only done one other card - their winning Pikachu entry for an illustration contest.

Which cards in this Pokémon TCG set are you most excited to open? Is there an Illustration Rare you think deserves more attention? Let us know over on the Wargamer Discord.

title: BattleTech Mech Overview: Spector
content:
Welcome back to the arena, sports fans! This is the Mech Overview you've all been waiting for, as we dig into all the crazy custom configurations fielded by Solaris's up-and-coming star of the 3066 season, the mysterious mercenary known as Spectre!

...wait, what's that?

We're not talking about the apocryphal protagonist of MechWarrior 4: Mercenaries today, we're actually looking at the 35-ton Spector? Dammit, what did I hire Duncan Fisher for, then?

Spector. Credit: Rockfish

The Spector originated as a miniature counterpart to the Exterminator, a relationship which is pleasantly visible in their modern redesigns; I always like it when you can really see a coherent design lineage in BattleTech. Where the Exterminator was effectively monopolized by ComStar, however (and has been nearly extinct since the Jihad), the Spector found a new lease on life in the 3050s through Lyran manufacturer Norse-Storm BattleMechs, and has actually proliferated fairly widely since then.

The Spector is another very consistent mech: It always has full armor coverage (in the same layout!) and an all-energy weapons loadout, it usually moves 7/11/7, and it usually has some form of stealth technology, though in some cases that's as simple as a basic Guardian ECM Suite.

What does all that add up to? Let's take a closer look!

Variants

These mechs have all been reviewed based on a standard F through S scale, which you can find described on our landing page here (along with all of our other ‘Mech reviews, the name of the box you can buy to get any of the mechs we have covered, and our general methodology).

Davion Heavy Guards Spector. Credit: Jack Hunter

SPR-4F

The original Star League Spector mounts both classic stealth technologies, a Chameleon Light Polarization System and a Null Signature System, along with a Guardian ECM, all that layered on top of a full load of standard armor on a standard chassis, with 7/11/7 movement from an XL engine and a base load of 10 Double Heat Sinks. Its teeth aren't particularly impressive... a regular Large Laser and two Medium Lasers aren't even a PSR's worth of damage... but if objectives beyond killing are in play, 1,224 BV for something this fast and hard to kill isn't the worst deal. The 4F does face the issue that its stealth systems alone build 16 heat if they're both active, meaning that on a full-distance jump with all its stealth tech turned on it builds three heat even without shooting anything, but if it drops the Null Sig, the CLPS + an Alpha Strike only builds movement heat, which isn't bad for a Jump 7 stealth mech.

This seems like a neat toy for objective play, but it is extremely extinct in the modern day if you're playing with MUL availability, and its fancy stealth systems can be countered the way nearly any stealth can be countered in this game: All you have to do is get closer to it.

Lynn's Rating: C?

SPR-5F

The revived Invasion-era Spector drops its LosTech stealth systems, swaps to Endo-Steel structure, and adds one heat sink and a small laser in the head. The emotional support small laser can actually come in clutch here under the right circumstances, pushing the 5F over the "can trigger a PSR on its own" threshold, and heat is no worry here: the 5F is heat neutral on a jumping alpha. I still can't call this mech impressive, exactly, but it's down to 1,183 BV, and for a bouncing ECM bubble with non-negligible damage output and the best armor its tiny body can support, that's not a terrible price.

Lynn's Rating: C+

Dawn Guard Spector. Credit: Jack Hunter

SPR-5S

The end result of some rather contentious dealing between Norse-Storm and Capellan manufacturer Shengli Arms, the 5S is a 5F which swaps to Stealth Armor and (for crit space reasons) consolidates the two medium lasers into one medium pulse laser. This manages, by just a hair, to be the lowest damage potential the Spector chassis ever sees, and with the stealth running it builds 1+movement heat on an alpha strike. Its cost has actually dropped further, though, down to 1,155 BV. I could see an argument in this mech's favor for objective play, but in the game of inches between largely similar Spector variants, I'm less impressed by this one.

Lynn's Rating: C-

SPR-ST

An oddball sidegrade of the 5S, the ST drops the jump jets in favor of MASC and replaces the mech's armaments with an ERLL and two ERMLs enhanced by a targeting computer. With the Stealth off, this builds movement heat on an alpha strike; with Stealth on, it either builds movement firing the ERLL or is neutral at a run firing the ERMLs.

Any increase in range is of benefit to a stealth mech, and extra accuracy is always welcome, but the BV of this variant shoots up to 1,438, and it simply doesn't do enough to justify that cost, in my opinion.

Lynn's Rating: D

SPR-6F

Okay, now this one's cooking. Built to counter the Lyrans' Clan opponents (and, ironically, adopted by the Tiburon Khanate of Clan Sea Fox), the 6F keeps nothing but the Endo-Steel skeleton of prior Spector models and overhauls everything else. With an uprated engine (still an Inner Sphere XL) and an additional jump jet to match, the 6F moves 8/12/8, and its armor load has switched over to Reflective. Its right arm gun has been replaced with a Medium Variable-Speed Pulse, the two lasers on the left arm are both Clan Improved Heavy Medium Lasers, it carries a Spheroid ERSL in its head For Some Fucking Reason, and it mounts a targeting computer (boosting that VSP to an unholy -4 TN in its short range band). Unfortunately, to find the mass for all that, it's saddled with a small cockpit. This Spector also drops the ECM, losing some utility.

This is the Spector I'm most familiar with, and it's a total transformation. Reflective Armor and a Small Cockpit are an unfortunate combination, and the 6F can't tape down the triggers (building 1+movement heat with its three medium lasers alone), and autocannons loaded with Precision can make it cry, but there is a significant amount of accurate damage here, and this thing laughs at pulse lasers. Its 1,476 BV cost feels pretty good presently, but when VSP costs get fixed in the upcoming BV update, this is one of the mechs which might suddenly become too rich for my blood. Get it while the getting's good!

Lynn's Rating: B

Spector. Credit: Valk

Final Thoughts

The Spector is very much two mechs in a trench coat. All of them other than the 6F are basically premium-priced objective dorks who trade off firepower in exchange for ECM coverage and decent survivability (though a precision AC/20 round to a side torso will make any Spector cease to exist, with their Inner Sphere XL engines). The 6F, meanwhile, is an aggressive backstabber competing in the same arena as the Tiburon 2 or Piranha 5, but it falls a little bit behind the curve in pure damage output due to the BV cost of its jump MP and Targeting Computer.

A Spector is unlikely to be the optimal choice for whatever job you have in mind for it from the standpoint of pure cost efficiency, but it's still a pretty capable guy, and the 6F is a singular entity in its particular combination of offense and defense.

Until next time, MechWarriors, this is Dunc- I mean, this is Lynn, signing off!

title: Games Industry News Roundup- August 4th, 2026
content:
Here at Tabletop Battles, we know that it’s hard to keep track of all the news happening all the time in the games industry. So much is always going on, all over the place, all the time. With games of all sorts, and their related media, being an informed gamer can feel impossible some days. 

That's why every week, we help you stay in the know by rounding up five of the biggest recent stories in the gaming and gaming-related pop culture sphere in the Games Industry News Roundup. Our trusty news boy, Dan “Swiftblade” Richardson, is right here at the very real, and cool TTB newsdesk with the scoop.

Leading Company in Card Grading Facing Giant Class Action Lawsuit

Credit: PSA

The Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA), the largest service in the world for card grading of all kinds, is the subject of a large class-action lawsuit accusing the card grading company of engaging in widespread fraud with its business practices. 

The lawsuit was filed in Baltimore last week by Nicholas Funk on behalf of thousands of people all over America who have used the service in the past. Funk accuses PSA of defrauding the public by engaging in “subjective” behavior while grading cards submitted for quality and value, despite advertising themselves as wholly impartial judges. 

“PSA sells card grading as an expert driven, criteria-based, unbiased, and reliable credential that the market treats as authoritative,” the lawsuit states. “It delivers something materially different. Its grading involves a subjective, opaque, inconsistent, financially conflicted system backed by an obscure online ‘contract’ that purportedly disclaims reliability, caps remedies, and forces arbitration. Consumers paid for expertise and reliability, but PSA sold them manufactured uncertainty and then charged them for it.”

Luck accuses PSA of engaging in this fraudulent grading practice since the very beginning of its existence in 1991 with the very first card ever submitted. The company gave out a "Near Mint-Mint 8" grade to a vintage Honus Wagner baseball card. The card would become the most famous and valuable card in the world, selling for $2.8 million in 2013. This is despite the fact the card was tampered with prior to its submission to PSA, which was later admitted by the owner of the card and, according to Luck, should have been clear during the grading process and greatly diminished the value of the card. The fact PSA still gave the card such a high grade only proves that the fraudulent grading practices of the company are systemic, and have been around from the very beginning.

The lawsuit alleges that since then, the PSA has focused on corporate profit over proper grading practices, engaging in anti-consumer activities like hiring contract temp labor without proper grading training during periods of high volume, giving preferable grades to recognizable players or characters, and artificially limiting the number of perfect 10 grades to increase their sell value.

While PSA hasn’t commented on Funk’s lawsuit, it did release a statement over the weekend regarding a different lawsuit from Steve Lichtmann, who sued the company over a 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle card he submitted for grading. 

“A grade is an expert opinion.” PSA stated in regard to Lichtmann’s lawsuit. “Its value to the hobby rests on the fact that specific grades cannot be bought, pressured, or litigated into existence. A grade obtained only by threatening a lawsuit would be worthless — to the market, and to the millions of collectors who trust PSA to treat every submission the same, whether it comes from a first-time hobbyist or a seasoned collector submitting a rare and sought-after item.”

While card grading initially focused on sports trading cards, its popularity with TCGs has exploded in the post-pandemic years, particularly in the world of Pokémon, and has been a large contributing factor to card shortages and secondary market price spikes.    

Dungeons & Dragons Set to Release “Mature Content” Expansion

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

It was Christmas in July for Dungeons & Dragons fans last week, as Wizards of the Coast revealed multiple new expansions for the hugely popular game, including officially acknowledging the leaked World of Warcraft expansion and announcing a Dark Sun setting book aimed at “mature audiences only.”

The World of Warcraft expansion was accidentally leaked by digital tabletop platform Roll20 in July with a pre-order announcement that was swiftly taken down. Following this, fans suspected that the full reveal for the book would arrive during GenCon last week, and Wizards didn’t disappoint. 

The new sourcebook, which is set to release later this fall, will let players explore the central setting of the WarCraft series, Azeroth. Alongside providing background for the iconic setting, the new book will also feature a litany of new content aimed directly at emulating characters, creatures, or concepts from the hit series. From what was revealed during the keynote, Dungeons & Dragons: World of Warcraft will include 13 new classes, 16 new playable races, over 50 new spells, and over 60 new creatures all based on the established lore of Azeroth.

While this isn’t the first time Wizards has released a crossover sourcebook in modern memory, the company is doing something very new with another one of its upcoming expansions. The long-running grim spinoff world, Dark Sun, will be receiving two new 5.5e books in early 2027, with one focused on the Dark Sun setting and the other focused on gameplay. These books will be “mature rated” books, a first for the current edition of the game, due to their graphic depictions of violence, nudity, and slavery. According to the Keynote announcement, these books will be shrink-wrapped on store shelves to “protect” audiences from their adult content.

While no specific release date was announced for Dark Sun, it’s slated as the first major D&D product for release in 2027. D&D: World of Warcraft is scheduled to release on November 17th, 2026.    

Missile Strike Destroys Ukrainian Board Game Distribution Center

Credit: Catan

The Ukrainian games publisher and distributor, Rozum, is in dire straits after a Russian missile struck its warehouse, destroying its entire stock of over 200,000 games.

Rozum is the largest publishing company for Ukrainian board game localizations since its founding in 2018, including multiple massively popular titles such as Catan, Exploding Kittens, and Power Grid. It has remained in continuous operation since, despite the ongoing invasion of Ukraine by the Russian military. 

The main warehouse for Rozum, located just outside the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv, was struck by a Russian ballistic missile on August 1st. According to Rozum’s parent company, Factor Group, there were fortunately no casualties suffered from the attack, but the stock of games stored in the building was completely lost, with estimated damages around $670,000.

“This blow is not only to cardboard boxes, but also to a cultural product that promotes the Ukrainian language, fosters a culture of shared leisure, brings people together in such difficult times, and educates children through play,” Factor Group wrote regarding the attacks. “Rozum Publishing is currently assessing the damage and planning its next steps. The company’s management assure us that they will definitely resume operations and continue to create popular board games for Ukrainians.”

Factor Group and Rozum launched a fundraising appeal for supporters to donate funds to help the company financially recover from the attack, and to reprint all the games destroyed. 

Last Sentinel Dev Team Hit with Layoffs; Game Stuck in Development Limbo

Credit: Lightspeed LA/Tencent

Remember The Last Sentinel? You know, from that one trailer at The Game Awards back in 2023? Of course you do, how could anyone forget? After a long silence following the game’s announcement, we finally have an update about the planned open world cyberpunk game, but unfortunately it's bad news. Despite some additional promotional videos last year, the game seems no closer to release, and the development team was hit with a large-scale layoff by its owner, Tencent.

According to reporting from Bloomberg, Last Sentinel, which was pitched as Tencent’s competitor to Grand Theft Auto, has been in development hell for six years, going through multiple builds and starting from scratch several times over, costing hundreds of millions of dollars in the process. In a recent statement from Lightspeed LA, the developers behind Last Sentinel, the most recent test build failed to impress players, forcing the team to once again start from square one with the project. 

“Because of this shift, some roles at the studio will be affected,” Lightspeed wrote on their LinkedIn. “We are treating affected team members with compassion and respect, offering comprehensive support and where possible the opportunity to transfer internally.”

While no official word on Last Sentinel’s fate has come from Lightspeed or Tencent, sources close to the issue told Bloomberg that Tencent informed Lightspeed LA leadership that it decided to not move forward with the project following the recent negative reactions to the test build.

While it’s possible we may still see a scaled-down version of Last Sentinel released in the future, or for its assets to be used in other games, its dream of becoming a competitor to Grand Theft Auto is very dead. 

EA Acquisition by Saudi Public Investment Fund Approved 

Credit: Electronic Arts

It’s even more bad news for the video games industry, which seems like the only news coming out of it nowadays. The final approvals by international regulatory bodies for the purchase of EA by the Saudi Public Investment Fund went through last week, with the deal set to close today, August 4th. 

The massive purchase of one of the largest publishers in gaming was announced in September of last year. With this deal, EA would be purchased for $55 billion by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), Silver Lake Capital, and Affinity Partners, with the Saudi PIF owning a little over 90% of the company shares. 

The deal was reviewed by regulatory bodies from all over the globe, including the SEC and EU Commission. The SEC would go on to approve the deal, as well as the EU Commission, with the EU writing that the acquisition “"would not raise competition concerns, given its limited impact on competition in the markets where the companies are active.”

Despite the assurances from EA leadership that the purchase wouldn’t cost EA employees their jobs, the company has already gone through several rounds of large layoffs this year in the lead up to the finalization of this deal, including a massive cut to the teams behind the commercial and critical success, Battlefield 6. While we will have to wait and see how things settle following the closure of this deal, it seems near certain that many more jobs will be lost as the publisher transitions to becoming privately owned.
